captions.text: Okay, tell me why.
Yes, it is intensely difficult to beat the market.
That's exactly why simple mechanical formulas and algorithms
ultimately fail during periods of stress because they break.
Exactly. Algorithms are entirely based on historical
data and predictable correlations.
They are, in a very real sense, the ultimate
first level thinkers just operating at light speed.
Oh wow, I never thought of it that way.
Yeah, they assume the future will look exactly like
the past. But as Joel Greenblat points out in
his annotations of the text, agreeing with the consensus
is a very comfortable place to be emotionally.
But it is not where above average profits are
found. You do not need a supercomput to beat
the market. You need the psychological discipline to look
at a compelling narrative on financial television and
ask yourself one simple question, which is,
and who doesn't know that?
Oh man, and who doesn't know that?
That is such a killer question.
It cuts through all the noise because if a
piece of information is on the front page of
the Wall Street Journal or, you know, being yelled
about on a cable news show, it is already
baked into the price of the stock.
Precisely. If everyone knows it, it is no longer
an advantage. It's useless.
Anformational advantage only exists when you know something the
crowd doesn't. Or more likely, when you analyze the
same information but draw a completely different conclusion because
you aren't blinded by the prevailing emotion of the
Right? So superior investing is at its absolute
core an exercise in second level thinking.
But you know knowing this in a vacuum doesn't
help unless we look at what happens when human
beings are actually put under pressure under extreme stress
cuz the market isn't a math equation.
It's a pendulum of human emotion.
And to apply this thinking you really have to
understand the environment you're operating in.
The environment is everything.
And let me tell you, it is incredibly hostile
to rational thought. Let's look at 1999.
